## Proof

**Setup and notation.** Let the polygon have $2n$ edges (the count is even since every edge of a closed surface is identified with exactly one partner). The $2n$ edges are partitioned into $n$ pairs; each pair yields one generator. Label these generators $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Traverse the boundary of the polygon once, cyclically, in a fixed direction. Each edge encountered is traversed either in the direction agreeing with its generator's chosen orientation (contributing $a_i$) or in the opposite direction (contributing $a_i^{-1}$). The resulting cyclic word
$$w = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_{2n}, \qquad x_k \in \{a_1, a_1^{-1}, \dots, a_n, a_n^{-1}\},$$
is the **boundary word** of the polygonal representation.

**Claim.** $\displaystyle \pi_1(P) \cong \langle\, a_1, \dots, a_n \mid w \,\rangle.$

**Proof via the CW-structure.** The quotient space $P$ inherits a CW-structure from the polygon:

- **0-skeleton:** By hypothesis all vertices of the polygon are identified to a single point $v$ in the quotient. Hence there is exactly one 0-cell, $v$.

- **1-skeleton:** Each identified pair of edges becomes a single 1-cell whose two endpoints are both $v$. Thus each 1-cell is a loop at $v$, and the 1-skeleton $P^{(1)}$ is a wedge (bouquet) of $n$ circles, one for each generator $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Consequently
$$\pi_1(P^{(1)}, v) \cong F(a_1, \dots, a_n),$$
the free group on $n$ generators, with basepoint $v$.

- **2-skeleton:** The interior of the polygon is a single 2-cell $D$. Its attaching map $\varphi : \partial D \to P^{(1)}$ traces the boundary of the polygon: it reads off the word $w = x_1 \cdots x_{2n}$ in the 1-skeleton, since each edge of $\partial D$ maps to the corresponding loop $a_i^{\pm 1}$.

**Applying Seifert–van Kampen.** The standard theorem for attaching a single 2-cell (a special case of Seifert–van Kampen, or equivalently the cellular theorem for CW-complexes with one 0-cell) states:

> If $X = X^{(1)} \cup_\varphi D^2$ is obtained from a path-connected space $X^{(1)}$ by attaching a 2-cell along $\varphi : S^1 \to X^{(1)}$, then
> $$\pi_1(X) \cong \pi_1(X^{(1)}) \,/\, \langle\!\langle [\varphi] \rangle\!\rangle,$$
> i.e. the normal closure of the attaching loop is killed.

Here $[\varphi] = w \in F(a_1, \dots, a_n) = \pi_1(P^{(1)})$. Therefore
$$\pi_1(P) \cong F(a_1, \dots, a_n) \,/\, \langle\!\langle w \rangle\!\rangle \cong \langle\, a_1, \dots, a_n \mid w \,\rangle.$$

**Why the single-vertex hypothesis matters.** If the vertices were not all identified, the 1-skeleton would be a general graph (not a wedge of circles), and one would have to choose a maximal tree $T$ in the 1-skeleton and quotient out the generators corresponding to edges of $T$ (each tree edge gives a trivial relation $a_i = 1$). The hypothesis "all vertices identified to a single point" forces the 1-skeleton to already be a bouquet, eliminating the spanning-tree step and leaving exactly one relator — the boundary word $w$.

**Summary.** The fundamental group of the polygonal representation $P$ has the presentation
$$\boxed{\pi_1(P) \cong \langle\, a_1, \dots, a_n \mid w \,\rangle,}$$
where $a_1, \dots, a_n$ are the $n$ generators corresponding to the $n$ identified edge-pairs, and $w$ is the boundary word obtained by reading the labels (with exponents $\pm 1$ according to orientation) of the $2n$ edges in cyclic order around the polygon.
